text:
Discover AI: A Learning Guide

A desktop app that teaches you how modern AI works by letting you play with it.

There are 62 small hands-on labs. In each one you move a slider, click a word, or train a tiny model, and you watch what changes. Next to every lab there is a short lesson that explains what you just saw. You can read it in short, simple sentences, in plain everyday words, or in the more technical version.

 Try it in your browser . There's nothing to install.

 

Watch the tour as a video for a sharper version.

 About

I wanted to create a single place for anyone to learn AI. One that runs on your own computer, keeps track of what you've learned, lets you challenge yourself when you're ready, and makes hard ideas easier to understand through visuals and hands-on play.

 What's inside

The 62 labs are split into seven groups. You can go in order or jump to whatever you're curious about.

 Group What you'll learn 
 --- --- 
 Start with the groundwork (1 to 8) What AI is, three math labs (vectors and matrices, slopes and gradients, probability and surprise), data and features, classic machine learning, the training loop, and how we know a model works 
 Build the foundations (9 to 17) Tokens and embeddings, a neural network whose parameters you turn like knobs, a single neuron, stacking neurons, loss and gradient descent, backpropagation, training dynamics, why GPUs matter, and the main model types 
 Look inside models (18 to 24) Next-token prediction, attention, the transformer block, the KV cache, attention at scale, scaling laws, and structured decoding 
 Build with a trained model (25 to 30) Search with embeddings, RAG, tools and function calling, agents, multimodal models, and failure modes and safety 
 Explore the frontier (31 to 39) Reinforcement learning, post-training, in-context learning and reasoning, diffusion, the AI ecosystem, ethics, interpretability, and what AGI and superintelligence mean 
 Pretrain a model (40 to 50) A full training run: splitting it across GPUs, building a dataset, synthetic data, hyperparameters, optimizers, training from scratch, evaluation, keeping a run stable, mixture-of-experts training, and mid-training with data mixtures 
 Adapt and ship a model (51 to 62) Fine-tuning, LoRA, model merging, training an embedding model, instruction tuning, preference tuning, reasoning models, RL environments for agents, quantization, distillation, serving, and a final "ship it" capstone 

 Screenshots

 Learning map. The home screen shows all seven groups of labs and how far you've got.

 

 Math foundations. Three labs cover vectors and matrices, slopes and gradients, and probability. Each one asks you to guess before it shows the answer, then lets you check the guess in the picture.

 

 3D you can turn. Five labs draw their idea in 3D: loss surfaces you can turn and press flat into a contour map, three optimizers walking one ravine, a training run as a block of GPUs, and words as points in space. Drag to turn any of them.

 

 Neural networks lab. Every parameter is a knob you can turn. Tune two by hand, then seven, then watch training turn them all at once, and count how many a real model has.

 

 AGI and superintelligence lab. Place real systems on a two-axis map where AGI and ASI are named cells, see one set of test scores give three answers to "is it AGI?", and run a small model of an intelligence explosion to see which assumptions make it run away.

 

 Attention lab. Click a word and see which other words it looks at. This one runs a real small transformer right in the app.

 

 Backpropagation lab, in dark theme. Step through the forward pass and then follow the gradients backward, one calculation at a time.

 

 Train one from scratch. Pick some text, a model size, and a training recipe. The model retrains on every change, so you can watch the loss fall and the samples get better.

 

 Optimizers lab. Train the same tiny model with SGD, momentum, AdamW and Muon on the same batches, then compare how far each one brings the loss down.

 

 Connections map. See how all 62 labs link together. Pick one to see what it builds on and what it leads to.

 

 Simple, Plain or Standard. The welcome tour shows the same idea written all three ways, so you can pick the one that suits you.

 

 Features

- 62 interactive labs. Each lab is split into a few short steps with a "Try this" hint, so you always know what to do next.
- Three ways to read. Simple mode uses short sentences an 8th grader can follow. Plain mode uses everyday words. Standard mode uses the proper technical terms. Switch at any time from the top bar.
- 3D pictures you can turn. Loss surfaces, a ravine with three optimizers on it, a block of GPUs and a cloud of words are drawn in 3D where a flat picture would hide the shape. Each one also has a flat view or the numbers beside it.
- Real models where it matters. The attention lab runs a small trained transformer in the app. The training labs train a tiny language model live while you watch.
- Checkpoints. Short quizzes at the end of each lab to check what stuck.
- Progress and bookmarks. Your progress is saved, and the Learn panel remembers where you stopped reading in each lab. Bookmark any section to come back to it later, or copy a link that opens the lab exactly as you left it.
- Search everything. Press Cmd+K on Mac or Ctrl+K on Windows and Linux to search labs, lessons, glossary terms, and settings.
- Optional AI guide. Ask questions about the lab you're on. Use a small model that runs on your computer, or connect your own OpenAI, Anthropic, or Google key. This is completely optional. Everything else works without it.
- Built to be easy on everyone. Light and dark themes, seven text sizes, high contrast, color-blind friendly palettes, reduced motion, keyboard support, and read-aloud.
- Private and offline. No account and no tracking. Lessons work without the internet, and your data stays on your computer.

install.title: Getting started
install.html:
The quickest way to try Discover AI is to open fazmin.github.io/AILearningGuide in your browser. All the labs and lessons work there.

To install the desktop app, download it from the latest release. Get the .dmg for macOS, the -setup.exe or .msi for Windows, or the .AppImage, .deb, or .rpm for Linux. The app isn't signed yet, so your computer will warn you the first time you open it. On a Mac, go to System Settings > Privacy & Security and click Open Anyway. On Windows, click More info, then Run anyway.

To run it on your own computer, you can use the web version or the desktop app. The desktop app gives you everything, including the local AI guide.

What you need
  • Node.js version 20.19 or newer (version 22 or newer is best)
  • Git
  • For the desktop app only: Rust and the Tauri prerequisites for your system
Option 1: Run the web version
git clone https://github.com/Fazmin/AILearningGuide.git
cd AILearningGuide
npm install
npm run dev

Then open http://localhost:1420 in your browser.

All the labs and lessons work here. The local AI guide and safe storage for API keys only work in the desktop app.

Option 2: Run the desktop app

First install the Tauri prerequisites for your system. Then:

git clone https://github.com/Fazmin/AILearningGuide.git
cd AILearningGuide
npm install
npm run tauri dev

The first run takes a few minutes because Rust has to compile everything. After that it starts much faster.

Build an installer

To make an app you can install and share:

npm run tauri build

You'll find the result in src-tauri/target/release/bundle/.

usage.title: How to use it
usage.html:
1. Pick a reading mode. The welcome tour asks if you want Simple, Plain or Standard. You can change it any time with the switch at the top.
  2. Open a lab. Start at lab 1 from the home screen, or pick any lab from the sidebar.
  3. Follow the steps. Each lab has a few steps at the bottom. Read the "Try this" hint, play with the controls, and see what happens.
  4. Read along. The Learn panel on the right explains what you're seeing. Use the contents bar at its top to jump between sections, bookmark the ones you want to come back to, and open the Glossary to look up key words, or use "Read out loud" to listen instead.
  5. Check yourself. Take the checkpoint at the end, then click "Mark complete".
  6. See the big picture. Open "Connections" in the sidebar to see how the labs fit together and what to learn next.
Setting up the AI guide (optional)

Open Settings in the desktop app.

  • Local model. One click downloads a small open model (Qwen3.5 2B, about 1.3 GB) and the llama.cpp engine to run it. Both files are checked before they run. After that the guide works fully offline and nothing you type leaves your computer.
  • Cloud providers. Add your own OpenAI, Anthropic, or Google API key if you prefer a bigger model. Keys are saved in your system's keychain, not in a file.

Once it's set up, click Ask the guide in any lab. The guide knows which lab you're on and what you're looking at.
